symbols.name: source length
symbols.meaning: The length of the Fourier transform to be replaced.
symbols.quote: Gaussian resampling expresses a Fourier transform of length $s$ through one of a nearby larger length $t$ (a power of two there), so that only power-of-two transforms need a fast algorithm.

symbols.name: Gaussian width parameter
symbols.meaning: An integer, with 2 <= alpha < sqrt p, that is the width parameter of the Gaussian weights.
symbols.quote: and let $\alpha$, the width parameter of the Gaussian weights below, be an integer with $2\le\alpha<\sqrt p$.

symbols.name: relative gap
symbols.meaning: The relative gap t/s - 1 between the two lengths.

symbols.name: coordinate selection
symbols.meaning: The map from C^t to C^s that selects coordinate q_j into position j.
symbols.quote: Let $C$ select coordinates from length-$t$ to length-$s$ vectors, $(Cv)_j=v_{q_j}$, and $(\mathsf Du)_j=e^{\pi\alpha^2\beta_j^2}u_j$.

symbols.name: exponent slack
symbols.meaning: A fixed constant 0 < delta < 1/8 that is the slack in the exponents of the time bounds.

symbols.name: output coordinate index
symbols.meaning: A coordinate index of a vector in C^t, taken modulo t.
symbols.quote: Define the permutations $(P_su)_j=u_{tj}$ and $(P_tv)_k=v_{-sk}$ (coordinate indices $j$, $k$ taken modulo $s$, $t$), which stay in the identity, never executed as sorts.

symbols.name: target length
symbols.meaning: The larger length, a power of two in the application, of the transform used instead of the length-s one.
symbols.quote: Gaussian resampling expresses a Fourier transform of length $s$ through one of a nearby larger length $t$ (a power of two there), so that only power-of-two transforms need a fast algorithm.

derivations.quote: Define the permutations $(P_su)_j=u_{tj}$ and $(P_tv)_k=v_{-sk}$ (coordinate indices $j$, $k$ taken modulo $s$, $t$), which stay in the identity, never executed as sorts.
In $(Nu)_j$, the summand with index $j$ is exactly $u_j$: the factor in $\mathsf D$ cancels the Gaussian factor at the selected coordinate $q_j$, because $tj/s-q_j=\beta_j$.
Since $\alpha^2<p$ and $\theta>p/\alpha^4$, $\alpha^2\theta>p/\alpha^2>1$, so $\|N-I\|<1/2$ and $N$ is invertible by the Neumann series $N^{-1}=\sum_i(-1)^i(N-I)^i$.
Set $\mathsf S'=\mathsf S/2$, $\mathsf J'=N^{-1}/2$, $\mathsf D'=2^{-(2\alpha^2-2)}\mathsf D$, and put $A=\mathsf S'$ and $B_0=\mathsf D'\mathsf J'C$.

The cited algorithms give approximations $\widetilde{\mathsf S}'$, $\widetilde{\mathsf J}'$, $\widetilde{\mathsf D}'$ with errors $16p$, $3p^2/4$, $4$ and times $O(tp^{3/2+\delta}\alpha)$, $O(tp^{3/2+\delta}\alpha)$, $O(tp^{1+\delta})$
The selection $C$ picks an ordered subsequence (since $t/s>1$), and the indices are generated in order with $O(p)$ work each, so $C$ takes $O(tp)$ time with zero error
Contraction of the exact maps yields errors less than $16p<p^2$ and $4+3p^2/4<p^2$ (as $p>100$), and the costs add to $O(tp^{3/2+\delta}\alpha)$.
The Neumann series with $E=N-I$ and $k=\lceil p/(\alpha^2\theta)\rceil$ is evaluated as $\widetilde{\mathsf J}'u=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(-1)^j\widetilde v^{(j)}$ with every iterate kept in $\mathbb D_p$.
